item.statement: Cost of irreps set by decomposition of the matrix-multiplication tensor; schoolbook algorithm
item.what_to_check: Strassen 1969; Blaser 2013 survey; Stander et al. 2024

chk.evidence:
The sentence at groups.tex:4 has no citation, and refs.bib has none of the candidate papers (11 entries).

Sources checked:
- Strassen 1969: bibliographic data confirmed from Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/BF02165411): "Gaussian elimination is not optimal", Numer. Math. 13(4):354-356. Springer's page is behind a login.
- Bläser 2013, "Fast Matrix Multiplication", ToC Graduate Surveys 5, pp. 1-60, doi 10.4086/toc.gs.2013.005. I fetched the landing page and the full PDF.
  - Sec. 1, Eq. (1.1): the standard algorithm "altogether uses n^3 multiplications".
  - Def. 4.4/4.5: the rank is the minimal number of products of linear forms, which equals the minimal number of triads.
  - Sec. 5: <k,m,n> is the matmul tensor.
  - Example 5.10: R(<2,2,2>)=7 (Strassen) and 19<=R(<3,3,3>)<=23.
- Shutman, Louidor, Tessler, arXiv 2509.06931 (fetched abs and html). Prop. 5.2: "Denote by m_d the tensor rank of matrix multiplication for real d×d matrices. Then ... rank(delta_{G,phi^{⊗3}}) <= m_d (type I), 3m_{d/2} (type II), 8m_{d/2} (type III)." They also note that the naive Gaussian implementation gives d_phi^3. Their setting is Hadamard/product nets trained with plain GD, with no norm or margin. This is the ML precedent for the claim that per-irrep width is set by the matmul tensor rank. What we add is the L_{2,b} norm price.
- Stander et al., ICML 2024 (PMLR 235:46441-46467): metadata confirmed. It is about coset circuits and does not support the tensor/schoolbook sentence.
- Chughtai et al. 2023 is already in the bib. Its GCR algorithm is the natural mechanistic citation for irrep matrix multiplication.

Caveat: the d^nu count for degree nu is our own generalisation of schoolbook's d^3. Strassen and Bläser only cover the bilinear case.

Notes: /Users/ruhaanrajadhyaksha/projects/grok/heracles/paper/litcheck/items/u7-group-tensor/CHECK.md. The web-search budget had run out, so every source came from direct fetches.

recommended_citations.why: Supports 'how cheaply the matrix-multiplication tensor can be written as a sum of products'. It is the canonical result that the matmul tensor decomposes more cheaply than schoolbook: 7 products for 2x2.

Textbook reference for tensor rank as the minimal number of products (Def. 4.4/4.5), for the schoolbook n^3 count (Sec. 1, Eq. 1.1) and for the matmul tensor <n,n,n> (Sec. 5). It supports the 'schoolbook algorithm' phrase.

Prop. 5.2 bounds the rank of each irrep's block by m_d, the tensor rank of dxd matmul, and notes that the naive algorithm gives d^3. It is the direct ML precedent for 'irrep cost = matmul tensor decomposition'. Their setting has no norm or margin, so our contribution is the norm price.

chk.recommended_change:
In groups.tex line 4, change "...a price set by how cheaply the matrix-multiplication tensor can be written as a sum of products; at even degree this is the schoolbook algorithm, with $d^
u$ neurons per $d$-dimensional representation." to "...a price set by how cheaply the matrix-multiplication tensor can be written as a sum of products \citep{strassen1969,blaser2013}; \citet{shutman2025} bound the width each irreducible representation needs by this tensor rank, and we add its price under the $L_{2,b}$ norm. At even degree the price is attained by the degree-$
u$ analogue of the schoolbook algorithm, with $d^
u$ neurons per $d$-dimensional representation." Optionally cite \citet{chughtai2023toy} (already in the bib) for irrep matrix multiplication in trained networks. Do not cite Stander et al. here; it belongs in the S5 empirics, as the coset-circuit contrast.
